items.answer: Empirical study is a usability-testing stage in interactive system development, performed after code testing, that systematically tests a fully implemented system with end users through a controlled experiment to collect and analyze data for assessing overall usability.

items.prompt: What is interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC)?
items.answer: Interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC) is a staged development method that is similar to regular software development but distinctive in its end-user requirement gathering, iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle, and empirical usability evaluation.

A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that can be built quickly to model or demonstrate a design idea and to test whether it will work in practice. It can be discarded after testing or refined into the final product.

Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.
User feedback is the involvement of users in different ways, not only through feedback, that iterations between stages in an interactive system development lifecycle account for.

Code testing is a standard software development stage in interactive system development that evaluates code as part of coding and implementation by ensuring it is bug-free and executes properly, but does not establish whether the system is usable.

questions.question: What characterizes the empirical evaluation stage in interactive system development?
options: Requirement collection by analysts for a developed system
Interface completion by designers for a developed system
Function verification by developers for a developed system
Usability judgment by end users for a developed system
questions.explanation: Empirical evaluation is the stage where end users judge the usability of the developed system. It is distinct from developer testing, requirement collection, or interface completion.

questions.question: Why is empirical evaluation placed after code testing in interactive system development?
options: Code testing checks the functional requirements and thereby confirms that the system is usable
Code testing compares the finished system with earlier prototypes and selects the better design
Code testing asks end users to try the finished system and report their problems
Code testing produces an executable system but does not establish that it is usable
questions.explanation: Code testing can show that the software runs, but it does not show that users can use it effectively, so a separate usability evaluation with users is needed after it.

data.text: Empirical evaluation is the interactive-system development stage where end users check a developed system's usability. It follows code testing, which produces an executable system but does not establish usability.
points: Empirical evaluation is a stage in interactive system development where end users evaluate a developed system's usability.
Empirical evaluation follows code testing, which produces an executable system but does not establish that it is usable.

questions.question: What can quick prototype evaluations quickly identify?
options: A final judgment about the entire system
Some major usability issues
A controlled comparison between end systems
A reliable conclusion about overall usability
questions.explanation: Quick prototype evaluations are limited early checks, so they can surface some major usability issues but cannot decide overall usability. A controlled comparison or reliable conclusion requires a fuller usability study.

questions.question: What kind of system must be evaluated for a conclusive overall usability judgment?
options: A code-tested but unimplemented design
A quick prototype of the system
A limited set of system features
The whole fully implemented system
questions.explanation: Conclusive usability assessment concerns the overall system, so it requires the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, partial feature set, or unfinished design.

questions.question: What method is needed to reach a reliable overall usability conclusion?
options: A feature comparison that lists and contrasts system capabilities
A controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data
A quick opinion survey that collects and analyzes user ratings
A code review that checks and verifies implementation defects
questions.explanation: A conclusive usability study is a controlled experiment, often called an empirical or usability study, that gathers and analyzes behavioral data from users. Opinions, code checks, or feature lists do not provide that behavioral evidence.

data.text: Quick prototype evaluations can surface some major usability problems early, but their small scale means they cannot decide the overall usability of the finished system. A conclusive assessment therefore evaluates the fully implemented system, preferably with more users, in a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes behavioral data. This controlled experiment is generally referred to as empirical research, an empirical study, a user study, or a usability study.
points: Quick prototype evaluations are limited early tests that can find some major issues but cannot conclusively assess overall end-system usability.
Conclusive usability assessment requires the fully implemented system, preferably more users, and a controlled experiment collecting and analyzing behavioral data.
A controlled experiment for usability evaluation is generally called empirical research, an empirical study, a user study, or usability study.

questions.question: What is the purpose of determining variables after the research questions in an empirical study?
options: To compare and evaluate several early prototypes
To design and execute a controlled experiment
To average and report several user opinions
To revise and check the research questions
questions.explanation: Variables are fixed after the research questions because they are what enable a controlled experiment to be designed and executed. Comparing prototypes, averaging opinions, or revising the questions do not serve that function.

data.text: An empirical usability study moves from questions to evidence. Research questions are set first, and variables are then determined because they are needed to design and execute a controlled experiment. The experiment is run to collect data, and objective analysis of that data is used to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability.
points: An empirical usability study follows four stages: research questions, variables, experiment, and objective analysis of usability data.

questions.question: What is the aim of an empirical usability study run after a system has been fully implemented?
options: The usability of a quick prototype
The usability of a design sketch
The usability of the interface
The usability of a requirement list
questions.explanation: An empirical study of a finished system is set up to collect and analyze data about the usability of that implemented interface. Prototype evaluations, requirements, and design sketches are not the target of such a post-implementation usability study.

questions.question: Why is formulating a research question the first stage of an empirical usability study?
options: The context of use is based on it
The hardware choices are based on it
The data analysis is based on it
The functional requirements are based on it
questions.explanation: The experiment is carried out to answer the research question, so the observations, data collection, and analysis are shaped by it. Earlier decisions such as requirements, hardware, or context of use are not what make the question the first stage of the study.

questions.question: When several users are asked whether a new text-entry GUI is good, what can the feedback look like?
options: The judgments split into quality levels
The judgments split into error levels
The judgments split into accuracy levels
The judgments split into speed levels
questions.explanation: Asking about whether the GUI is good can produce divided quality judgments, such as some users saying good, others poor, and one in between, so no definitive conclusion follows. The example is about quality judgments, not speed, errors, or accuracy.

data.text: An empirical usability study is conducted after implementation as an experiment that produces data for measuring usability. The study begins with a research question, since the experiment, observations, and analysis are all organized around answering it. The text-entry interface example shows why asking whether the new text-entry interface is good can produce divided judgments and no usability conclusion.
points: An empirical usability study tests a fully implemented system by setting up an experiment, running it, and collecting data.
The first stage of an empirical usability study is to formulate a research question guiding the experiment and analysis.
Asking whether the new text-entry graphical user interface is good can produce divided judgments and no usability conclusion.

questions.question: What keeps a question about whether a text input interface is better than Microsoft Word from reaching a definitive quality conclusion?
options: the term better can mean the same feature count to different users
the term faster can mean more or fewer features to different users
the term better can mean more or fewer features to different users
the term better can mean more or fewer errors to different users
questions.explanation: A better-than comparison is not definitive because different users may attach different feature-count meanings to better. The speed wording is not the reason, and a fixed feature count is not what the fact describes.

questions.question: What makes a question about whether a new text input interface is faster than Microsoft Word less subjective than a question about whether it is better?
options: It has users complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on speed
It has users complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on comfort
It has users complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on features
It has users complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on preference
questions.explanation: Asking about speed frames the comparison around completing a text input task and comparing performance on speed. Comparing features, comfort, or preference would leave the judgment tied to users' broader quality ideas.

questions.question: Why can a clear question about which text entry interface is faster still require an objective experiment?
options: Users' subjective speed answers can be made definitive by comparing two feature lists, whereas logged characters per minute can be compared directly
Users' subjective speed answers can be made definitive by asking each user twice, whereas logged characters per minute can be compared directly
Users' subjective speed answers can split, whereas logged characters per minute can be compared directly
Users' subjective speed answers can be made definitive by using a familiar text, whereas logged characters per minute can be compared directly
questions.explanation: Even a clear faster-than question can receive split subjective responses, so the experiment logs each user's characters per minute and compares those values directly. Repeating the question, choosing a familiar text, or comparing features does not remove that uncertainty.

data.text: Sharpening a usability question means comparing a proposed text-entry interface with Microsoft Word rather than evaluating it alone, but 'better' can still mean different features to different users. A speed-based question—whether a user can enter text faster with the new interface than with Microsoft Word—is less subjective, although user responses may still split. The experiment therefore has all users enter the same text and compares their character-per-minute rates to establish which interface is faster.
points: RQ2 is more concrete than standalone evaluation because it compares the interface with Microsoft Word, but 'better' is user-dependent.
RQ3 asks whether text entry is faster than Microsoft Word, making it less subjective than a vague quality question.
Subjective feedback may split, so the experiment uses the same text and compares characters per minute objectively.

questions.question: What makes a research question testable?
options: It allows a broad term such as good to cover several aspects of the system at once
It allows users' opinions to be collected and conclusions to be drawn after subjective interpretation
It avoids collecting data by relying on a single researcher's judgment of the interface
It allows objective data to be collected and conclusions to be drawn without subjective interpretation
questions.explanation: A testable research question supports a study that yields objective data and conclusions independent of users' subjective interpretation. The other options describe reliance on opinion, broad framing, or no data collection, which do not make a question testable.

questions.question: Why can a question about whether an interface is good not be directly tested objectively?
options: because it depends on comparing the interface with an existing alternative
because it depends on assigning fixed levels to the interface factor
because it depends on users' subjective interpretation and feedback
because it depends on logging text entry speed in characters per minute
questions.explanation: A generalized question about whether something is good cannot be directly tested objectively because it rests on users' subjective interpretation and feedback. The other options describe steps that can appear in an objective experiment, not the reason this broad question is untestable.

questions.question: Why may the answer to "Does interface A let users enter text faster than interface B?" not answer "Is A better than B?"?
options: because a faster interface is by definition a better interface
because speed and overall goodness refer to the same concept
because the broader question becomes testable once the interfaces are compared
because speed addresses one aspect rather than overall goodness
questions.explanation: Faster performance is one specific, measurable aspect, while better is a broader judgment that can include other aspects. Comparing two interfaces does not make the broader question testable by itself.

questions.question: How can a broader untestable usability question be addressed in stage 1 of an empirical study?
options: by applying a set of generic usability rules and treating them as the main questions
by framing multiple testable questions covering different aspects and combining their conclusions
by selecting one testable aspect and using its single result as the broader judgment
by framing one generalized question that is expected to cover the whole system in one pass
questions.explanation: To balance testability and generalization, an empirical study can frame several testable questions about different aspects and combine their conclusions toward a broader untestable usability question. A single broad question, a single narrow result, or generic design rules do not provide that structure.

data.text: Testable research questions, or hypotheses, allow studies to collect objective data and draw objective conclusions, while non-testable questions depend on subjective interpretation. Broad concepts such as “good” are ambiguous, so studies prefer specific testable questions instead. Stage 1 of an empirical study frames several testable questions about different aspects and combines their conclusions to answer a broader untestable usability question.
points: A testable research question, or hypothesis, permits collecting objective data and drawing conclusions independent of users' subjective interpretation.
A non-testable research question, also untestable, depends on subjective interpretation, so controlled experiments generally cannot draw reliable conclusions.
Research questions should avoid generalized concepts like “good” because they create untestable questions; testable questions support reliable, definite conclusions.
A specific testable question, such as whether an interface is faster, may not answer the broader question whether it is better.
Stage 1 of an empirical study frames multiple testable questions about system aspects and combines conclusions for a broader untestable question.

questions.question: In an empirical usability experiment, what is an independent variable?
options: A value that an interface factor can take in the experiment
A variable whose measured value depends on an interface factor in the experiment
A user characteristic that varies between participants in the experiment
A variable whose values are assigned and controlled in the experiment
questions.explanation: An independent variable, also called a factor, is the one whose values are assigned and controlled. A dependent variable is measured as an outcome, and a level is a value taken by a factor.

questions.question: How do factors and levels determine the test conditions in an experiment?
options: Each level of a dependent variable gives one test condition in the experiment
Each user characteristic gives one test condition in the experiment
Each factor gives one test condition without using its levels in the experiment
Each level of a factor gives one test condition in the experiment
questions.explanation: A factor’s levels are its assigned values, and each level becomes one test condition in which the dependent variable is observed. A dependent variable or a user characteristic does not supply the factor’s test conditions.

questions.question: Why is text entry rate called a dependent variable in the text-entry research question?
options: Because it is a condition used to observe interface performance in the experiment
Because its value depends on the interface levels in the experiment
Because it is a value assigned to the interface factor in the experiment
Because it is a user characteristic compared between participants in the experiment
questions.explanation: A dependent variable is one whose measured value depends on an independent variable’s levels. Here, text entry rate depends on which interface level is being tested.

data.text: For an empirical usability experiment, an independent variable, also called a factor, has values that are assigned and controlled, and those values are the factor's levels. A factor combined with its levels defines the test conditions. A dependent variable is the outcome whose value depends on those levels, such as text entry rate depending on interface levels.
points: An independent variable, also called a factor, has values that are assigned and controlled.
The values assigned to an independent variable or factor are called its levels.
Factors combined with their levels define an experiment's test conditions.
A dependent variable's value depends on an independent variable's levels, as text entry rate depends on interface levels.

questions.question: What is meant by empirical evaluation in XR development?
options: Observation of a virtual reality system's performance in the real world
Definition of an interactive system in the real world
Specification of a context of use in the real world
Observation of real users in the real world
questions.explanation: Empirical evaluation is observation of real users in the real world, not observation of system performance or work on specifications and definitions. The defining feature is that real users are observed in real-world conditions.

questions.question: How does research question framing handle a broad, untestable question about an interface?
options: Framing multiple testable questions and combining their conclusions
Choosing a single testable question and reporting its conclusions
Collecting subjective feedback and forming general conclusions
Asking one untestable question and accepting users' conclusions
questions.explanation: A broad untestable question is addressed by deriving several testable questions, collecting objective data for each, and combining the definite conclusions. A single untestable question or subjective feedback alone cannot support a reliable general conclusion.

questions.question: In an empirical study, how do independent variables differ from dependent variables?
options: Independent variables depend on results, and dependent variables are fixed at levels
Independent variables are measured scores, and dependent variables are assigned levels
Independent variables can take levels, and dependent variables depend on those levels
Independent variables are user judgments, and dependent variables are assigned levels
questions.explanation: Independent variables, also called factors, are the conditions that can take levels, while dependent variables depend on those levels. Reversing the roles, or treating the dependent variable as something that is set, is incorrect.

data.text: An empirical usability evaluation observes real users in the real world after the system is fully implemented, giving an overall picture of usability. Its empirical research process has four stages, with research question framing and variables as the first two. Research question framing turns untestable broad questions into testable questions, collects objective data, and combines definite conclusions, while the variables stage identifies independent variables, or factors, and dependent variables that depend on those factors and levels to design an experiment.
points: Empirical evaluation, or usability research, observes real users in the real world after full implementation to judge overall usability.
Empirical research has four stages, starting with research question framing and then variables.
Research question framing converts untestable broad questions into testable ones, uses objective data, and combines definite conclusions.
The variables stage identifies independent variables, or factors, and dependent variables that depend on factors and levels for an experiment.

options: Data Analysis
Variable Identification
Research Question Framing
Code Testing
items.reason: Research question framing, variable identification, and data analysis are stages of an empirical study, while code testing is an earlier stage of interactive system development.

activities.title: Order the stages of an empirical usability study

items.title: Order the stages of an empirical usability study
steps: Formulating the research questions for the study
Determining the variables and levels for the experiment
Designing and executing the experiment to collect data
Analyzing the data to reach usability conclusions

questions.question: Why must code testing be followed by an empirical study rather than serving as the final check of an interactive system?
questions.reference_answer: Code testing only checks that code is bug-free and executes, so it does not establish whether end users find the system usable. An empirical study follows it as a separate stage in which end users evaluate the developed system. Thus the system can be executable while still needing this user-based usability assessment.

questions.question: Why are quick prototype evaluations insufficient for a conclusive judgment about the overall usability of a fully implemented system?
questions.reference_answer: Quick prototype evaluations use a limited number of evaluators and prototypes, so they can identify some major usability issues but cannot give a conclusive result about the end system. A conclusive assessment requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment collecting and analyzing user behavioral data. The empirical study is carried out at the end, when the system is fully implemented, to obtain an idea of the overall usability.

questions.question: Why can a testable research question support a definite scientific conclusion when a non-testable research question generally cannot?
questions.reference_answer: A non-testable question depends on users' subjective interpretation and feedback, so a controlled experiment cannot be set up to collect objective data and generally no reliable conclusion can be drawn. A testable question allows a study to collect objective data and draw conclusions independently of subjective interpretation. Therefore testable questions should be used because they support reliable, definite scientific conclusions.

questions.question: In the variables stage of an empirical study, how do independent variables and dependent variables define the experiment for a text entry research question?
questions.reference_answer: The variables stage identifies the variables in the testable question to design the experiment. The independent variable, interface, has levels such as the course's design and MS Word, and these levels give the test conditions. The dependent variable, text entry rate, depends on those interface levels.
